actions.justification: Mandatory first step to establish baseline vital signs for this patient presenting with severe wheezing and dyspnea.
Mandatory assessment to determine oxygen saturation and guide oxygen therapy decisions in this asthmatic patient.
Mandatory assessment to quantify airflow obstruction severity in this asthma exacerbation patient.

Mandatory action: classify asthma exacerbation severity based on vitals, SpO2, PEF, and clinical presentation to guide appropriate treatment pathway. Patient has aspirin-sensitive asthma which is an important comorbidity to factor in severity assessment.

Continuous monitoring of HR, SpO2, RR is essential during acute asthma exacerbation to detect deterioration early, especially given aspirin-sensitive asthma comorbidity which can cause severe bronchospasm.
IV access should be established early in acute asthma exacerbation to enable rapid drug administration if patient deteriorates, including systemic corticosteroids or magnesium sulfate if needed.
Guideline-recommended O2 therapy for acute asthma targets SpO2 94-98%. High-flow O2 is not indicated as SpO2 is already 98%. Titrated oxygen prevents both hypoxemia and hypercapnia.

Continuous nebulized salbutamol (albuterol) is first-line bronchodilator therapy for acute asthma exacerbation per ATS/GINA guidelines. Patient has severe wheezing and dyspnea requiring immediate bronchodilation.

Assessing inhaler technique is important in asthma management to optimize bronchodilator delivery and identify potential contributors to the current exacerbation, especially relevant for ongoing care planning.

Ipratropium bromide nebulized is a key component of acute asthma management alongside salbutamol. Adding anticholinergic bronchodilation provides additive benefit in moderate-to-severe acute asthma per guidelines.

Systemic corticosteroids are recommended early in acute asthma exacerbations to reduce airway inflammation and shorten recovery. IV hydrocortisone is appropriate given acute presentation with severe wheezing.

Heliox (helium-oxygen mixture) reduces airway resistance and improves gas exchange in severe asthma with significant wheeze. Particularly beneficial in this patient given ongoing respiratory distress despite initial bronchodilator therapy.

Patient has asthma with aspirin-sensitive asthma. SpO2 is currently 98% on current therapy; however, supplemental oxygen support should be maintained. High-flow oxygen can support oxygenation during ongoing bronchospasm management.

Patient has aspirin-sensitive asthma with severe wheezing and dyspnea. Nebulized epinephrine can provide additional bronchodilation in refractory or severe asthma not fully responsive to salbutamol and ipratropium already administered.

Ketamine has bronchodilatory properties and is indicated as an adjunct in severe refractory asthma. Given ongoing severe wheezing despite bronchodilators and steroids already administered, ketamine infusion is a guideline-supported escalation step.

Magnesium sulfate IV is indicated for severe/refractory asthma exacerbation as a bronchodilator adjunct. Patient has aspirin-sensitive asthma and has already received multiple bronchodilator treatments; magnesium sulfate is a guideline-supported next step in refractory or severe acute asthma.

IV corticosteroids are a cornerstone of acute asthma management. Hydrocortisone IV has been given, but methylprednisolone IV may be appropriate as a continuation/alternative systemic steroid to reduce airway inflammation.
At 75 minutes into the encounter with ongoing severe asthma management, disposition planning (ICU vs ward vs discharge) should be assessed based on response to treatment so far.

Salbutamol nebulization is a first-line bronchodilator for acute asthma exacerbation. Although continuous salbutamol has been given, further doses may be needed given ongoing wheezing and dyspnea in this asthma patient.

Systemic corticosteroids are recommended in acute asthma exacerbations to reduce airway inflammation. IV methylprednisolone/hydrocortisone have been given; transitioning to or supplementing with systemic corticosteroid (oral or IV) supports continued anti-inflammatory therapy per asthma guidelines.

Patient has asthma with severe wheezing and dyspnea. Salbutamol via pMDI with spacer is a guideline-recommended bronchodilator delivery method for acute asthma, and has not been administered yet (continuous nebulized salbutamol already done, but pMDI/spacer is a distinct delivery method that can be used for ongoing bronchodilation).

Oral prednisolone is indicated for acute asthma as systemic corticosteroid therapy to reduce airway inflammation. While IV corticosteroids have been given, oral prednisolone provides continued steroid coverage and is part of standard acute asthma management per guidelines.

Patient with acute severe asthma requiring multiple bronchodilator and corticosteroid treatments needs inpatient admission for monitoring and continued management. SpO2 is currently 98% and vitals are stable, suggesting ward-level care is appropriate rather than ICU at this time.
